newsitem.title: Jordan: Hamas leader back in Amman, to engage in politics.
newsitem.headline: Hamas leader back in Amman, to engage in politics.

text.p: Musa Abu Marzook, political leader of the militant Palestinian movement Hamas, pledged on Tuesday to continue to work for the organisation after his release from nearly two years of detention in a New York jail.
"I will continue in political activities. Naturally the motives that made me stand with the hopes and aspirations of my people still exist," Abu Marzook told a news conference at his home in Amman.

"I have still a lot to do to serve my people and help them achieve their aspirations," said a beaming Abu Marzook, flanked by senior members of Hamas leadership in exile, all Jordanian citizens of Palestinian origin.
Abu Marzook returned to Jordan on board a special U.S. military plane which landed at Amman military airport late on Monday.
He had been expelled by Jordan in 1995 under pressure from Washington, Israel and the Palestinians and was arrested in the United States shortly afterwards.

Israel accused Abu Marzook, born in Gaza in 1951, of controlling the leadership of Hamas's military wing responsible for attacks killing scores of Israelis between 1990 and 1994. Hamas staunchly opposes Israeli-Palestinian peace deals championed by Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.

At the news conference Abu Marzook refused to condemn acts of violence against Israelis. "Palestinians had no choice but to fight for their rights as long as Israel was not ready to concede them," he said.
"If my Palestinain people gain their rights and settle their problems by peaceful solutions that is the best...the Palestinian people are desperate for peace more than any other nation."
Abu Marzook thanked Jordan's King Hussein for welcoming him back to Jordan. He said Arafat had called his family to congratulate them on his release.

An agreement signed with U.S. authorities two weeks ago, which he had to keep secret until he had left the United States, committed Washington not to "exert any pressure on any government as regards my future work or presence", Abu Marzook said.
But the Hamas leader said he signed a commitment not to go back to the United States.

He was deported to Jordan after Israel, which originally asked for his extradition to stand trial, dropped its request on security grounds, forcing the U.S. authorities to seek a country that could accept him.
Jordan says its decision to admit Abu Marzook was a purely humanitarian gesture by King Hussein with no strings attached except abiding by Jordanian law.
Abu Marzook, who plans to settle in Amman where many other Hamas leaders live, noted that Jordanian law did not prevent any citizen or resident from exercising his right of political expression.

Although his activities will be closely monitored by the authorities, Abu Marzook will feel at home in a country where a large section of the population are Palestinian refugees who settled there after the creation of Israel in 1948.
Abu Marzook, who is a stateless person with an Egyptian travel document given to Palestinian refugees from Gaza, dismissed the possibility of again being deported from Jordan.
"My departure from Jordan was under pressure from the American government...and my return back was at the request of the United States and it's not logical this case could be repeated," he said.
